name: False consensus effect
statement: People overestimate how many others share their own choice, so whichever option you would pick is the one you expect most people to pick.
meaning: The measurement is comparative rather than absolute, which is what makes it a bias rather than an opinion. Two people are asked the same question about what most others would do. One of them would choose option A and one would choose option B, and each gives a higher estimate for their own option. Neither estimate can be checked against the truth for that individual, but they cannot both be right, and the gap between them is the effect. Ross and colleagues framed it as egocentrism in social perception: your own response is the most available piece of evidence you have about what people do.

origin.who: Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House
origin.note: Their paper names the effect in its title, in quotation marks, which is how a phrase enters a literature. The best-known scenario asks whether you would walk around campus wearing a sandwich board reading REPENT.

evidence: 320 Stanford undergraduates, 80 to each of four stories, read a hypothetical situation ending in a two-way choice. They estimated what percentage of their peers would take each option, then stated their own choice. Averaging the four stories unweighted, the 186 who picked the first option put its popularity at 65.7%, and the 134 who picked the second put it at 48.5%, F(1,312) = 49.1, p < .001. Many Labs 2 converts that statistic to d = 0.79, 95% CI [0.56, 1.02]. A meta-analysis of 115 hypothesis tests eight years later put the effect at r = 0.31 across a range of paradigms. That figure is quoted here from Many Labs 2, because Mullen and colleagues' paper is paywalled and was not read for this entry. Whether the effect survives correction is disputed. Krueger and Clement ran three experiments in 1994 and found the bias held among participants who had been taught about it and among those given feedback on the real consensus. Engelmann and Strobel paid subjects for accurate estimates and separated the two readings. Eighty participants in five sessions of 16 chose between two options and then estimated eleven other subjects' choices, having been shown four of those choices in half the rounds. On the classical comparison a consensus effect appeared in 29 of the 32 cells that allowed one. On the stricter comparison it did not: the regression weight on a subject's own choice was 1.33 against 1.73 on the information about others, which is underweighting rather than overweighting.

replication.headline: Many Labs 2 ran two of the original scenarios across 125 samples in 36 countries and found the effect larger than the original both times.
replication.detail: The supermarket vignette produced d = 1.18 across 7,205 participants, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.13 to 1.23. The traffic-ticket vignette produced d = 0.95 across 7,827 participants, interval 0.90 to 1.00. Both are above the original d = 0.79 for the four scenarios pooled. Both are also above the scenario-specific originals the same paper prints, d = 0.99 for the supermarket and d = 0.80 for the traffic ticket, each of which carries a 95% interval whose lower bound is 0.00. The replication intervals are narrow enough to be a measurement rather than an estimate. Across the project, 21 of the 28 effects came back smaller than the original and seven larger, and 13 returned a null result or an effect in the opposite direction.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: The figures above are for the supermarket scenario; the traffic-ticket scenario in the same project gave 0.95. The site and participant counts are that scenario's, not the project's 125 samples and 15,305 people, because each protocol went to about half the samples. Many Labs 2 ran the supermarket vignette in 64 of them. Many Labs 2 also misreports the study it is replicating. Its summary gives the original consensus estimates as 75.4% and 54.9%. Those two numbers are Ross and colleagues' trait ratings, printed in a different table of the same paper; the consensus estimates are 65.7% and 48.5%. The d = 0.79 is derived from the F statistic and is unaffected. There is also an old and unresolved argument about what the effect measures. Robyn Dawes argued in 1989 that the usual definition does not earn the word false, because treating one's own choice as a sample of size one is sound inference. On that reading the effect is an error only where the own choice carries more weight than a stranger's would, and the original experiments do not separate the two. Dawes's paper is paywalled, OpenAlex and Unpaywall list no repository copy, and it was not read for this entry. The account of it here is Engelmann and Strobel's, who restate his argument and his stricter definition in full.
misreadings: The effect is often stated as people believing everyone agrees with them, which is stronger than the data. In the replication, participants who chose the first option put it at 69% and those who chose the second put it at 43%: both groups are well inside plausible ranges, and the finding is the difference between them. It also gets treated as an explanation for political polarisation on its own, where the evidence is about two-way choices in vignettes with nothing at stake. And it is regularly confused with the false uniqueness effect, which points the other way and shows up most on abilities. The two are not mirror images and they are not exclusive. Campbell found a reliable consensus effect on abilities as well as opinions, larger on opinions, with consensus overestimated for low abilities and underestimated for high ones. Monin and Norton found both errors in one field study of 415 people, run across the five days of a shower ban. Social projection, entry 548, is the same habit measured a third way, as a within-person correlation between what someone endorses and what they estimate for a group; Robbins and Krueger's meta-analysis of that measure gives r = .46 for ingroups against .13 for outgroups. This entry is filed alongside assumed similarity bias, entry 321, and the two are different measurements rather than two names for one finding. This effect compares the population estimates of two groups who chose differently on a two-way item, and no particular other person is being judged. Assumed similarity correlates a perceiver's self-description with their description of a named target, which is why Cronbach's 1955 analysis of that score is about components no consensus estimate contains.

The version read is the working paper of 8 July 1999 in the Humboldt University repository, not the journal article; the figures quoted here are that version's.
